1) What the code computes. runBacktest (src/App.jsx 1533-1541) calculates only beta, trackingError, treynor, alpha, infoRatio, sharpe, annPortReturn and annSpyReturn. setBacktestResult (1559-1565) adds portCum, spyCum, dates, corrMatrix, tickers and yearsBacktest. None of these is a drawdown, volatility, CAGR, Sortino or Calmar figure. Grepping App.jsx for drawdown|sortino|cagr|calmar finds nothing. "Volatil" appears only in the Sharpe optimizer's portStats (1367-1373, shown at 3264/3291), the VIX insight (661) and a scoring comment (354-362), never in the backtest. backend.py has no drawdown or Sortino code either. The screen (4359-4372) shows six cards: Tracking Error, Treynor, Beta, Jensen's Alpha, Sharpe, Information Ratio. Five of the six depend on the benchmark; only Sharpe does not. The glossary (4424-4431) covers the same six.

2) The finance reasoning holds. Max drawdown and CAGR are the most intuitive risk and return measures for retail users. Sortino counts only downside deviation, which fits how investors feel losses. Portfolio Visualizer and similar tools show CAGR, standard deviation, max drawdown, Sharpe and Sortino as standard.

3) A problem the finding misses. The "anual" returns shown in the banner (4350-4351) and the "Superando/Por debajo del benchmark" verdict (4291: outperforms = annPortReturn > annSpyReturn) use a simple average of weekly returns times 52 (1540-1541). That is not CAGR. Volatility drag (compound return is roughly the average minus σ²/2) means a volatile portfolio can show a higher "annual" return than SPY while ending lower on the cumulative chart right above it. So the banner can contradict the chart. This makes adding CAGR more than a nice extra.

4) Details the proposed fix needs:
(a) Real dates. fetchChart (129-147) returns only closes, and the backend /chart payload (backend.py 513) has no dates. The `dates` labels (1525-1531) are made up by counting back 7 days from today. The `.filter(isFinite)` at 1475/1487 can also drop points silently, shifting series against each other. A drawdown date range or recovery date built from these labels would be approximate at best.
(b) statCard (4293) takes only (label, value, unit). Every call passes a 4th color argument that is ignored, so all cards render in var(--accent). Any color-coding for new metrics needs this fixed first.
(c) Sortino's downside deviation must divide by the total number of weeks N, not just the weeks below the target. Calmar is traditionally measured over 36 months; CAGR/|MDD| over the whole period is the common variant and should be labeled that way.
(d) Style. calcSharpe uses the population standard deviation (/n) while calcTrackingError and calcPortfolioBeta use the sample version (/(n-1)). New metrics should pick one and stick to it.

Severity medium is fair for the missing metrics. The mislabeled arithmetic "annual" return driving the outperformance verdict could reasonably be rated high.
findings.corrected_fix:
A. Backend. In backend.py around line 513, also return dates: {"closes": closes, "dates": [d.strftime('%Y-%m-%d') for d in hist.index], ...}, keeping them aligned with closes after the MXN conversion and dropna. In the frontend, change fetchChart so it returns {closes, dates}. In runBacktest, join each ticker to SPY by date, not by trailing index, so dates are real. Then replace the synthetic labels at 1525-1531 with the real dates.

B. Pure helpers next to cumulativeReturns (~line 302). Wealth index W_t = Π(1+r), starting at W_0 = 1.
- cagr = W_T^(52/N) − 1
- annVol = sampleStd(r)·√52, using (n−1) consistently
- drawdown series dd_t = W_t / max_{s≤t} W_s − 1
- mdd = min(dd), with its peak index, trough index and recovery index (first t after the trough where W_t ≥ the peak W, or null meaning "sin recuperar")
- sortino: rfW = rf/52; DD = sqrt( Σ min(0, r_t − rfW)² / N ) over all N weeks; sortino = (mean(r) − rfW)/DD·√52
- calmar = cagr/|mdd|, labeled "Calmar (periodo completo)"
- bestWeek = max(r), worstWeek = min(r), pctPositive = count(r > 0)/N
Compute all of these for both portReturns and spyReturns after line 1541 and add them to setBacktestResult (1559-1565), e.g. portStats:{cagr,annVol,mdd,mddPeak,mddTrough,mddRecovery,sortino,calmar,bestWeek,worstWeek,pctPositive,ddSeries}, and spyStats:{...} with the same fields.

C. Headline correctness. At 4291 base `outperforms` on CAGR (portStats.cagr > spyStats.cagr), or on the last value of portCum vs spyCum. In the banner at 4350-4351 show CAGR as "anual compuesto". If the arithmetic figure is kept, label it "promedio aritmético anualizado".

D. UI. Change statCard at 4293 to (label, value, unit, color) and use color for the number. Then:
- Show a first row of retail-friendly cards, portfolio vs SPY: CAGR, Volatilidad anual, Máx. caída (with approximate peak→trough dates and recovery time), Sortino, Calmar.
- Move the benchmark-relative cards (TE, Treynor, Beta, Alpha, IR) into a second "vs benchmark" row.
- Below the cumulative LineChart (4327-4333), reuse LineChart with series [{name:"Mi Portafolio", data: portStats.ddSeries}, {name:"SPY", data: spyStats.ddSeries}] as an underwater (drawdown) chart. It already draws the dashed zero line when minY < 0; ideally fill the area toward 0 instead of toward the bottom edge.
- Add CAGR, Volatilidad, Máx. drawdown, Sortino and Calmar to the glossary (4424-4431).
- Optional: a 52-week rolling beta or Sharpe chart.

findings.title: Negative valuation multiples score as 'cheap' (EV/EBITDA, P/B, P/E lack the >0 guard that P/FCF has)
findings.evidence: 327: `if (pe != null) val += pe < 12 ? 2.5 : ...`. 330: `if (evEbitda != null) val += evEbitda < 8 ? 1.5 : ...`. 331: `if (pb != null) val += pb < 1 ? 1 : ...`. 366: `tech += pb < 1.5 ? 0.8`. Compare 332: `if (pcf != null && pcf > 0)`. The backend passes Yahoo's `enterpriseToEbitda` and `priceToBook` through unchanged (backend.py 286, 318), and both can be negative.
findings.why: A negative EV/EBITDA means negative EBITDA, a negative P/B means negative book equity, and a negative P/E means losses. None of these makes a stock cheap. As written, a loss-making or negative-equity company gets the maximum valuation points (+1.5 EV/EBITDA, +1 P/B, +0.8 technical), which can flip a SELL into HOLD or BUY. The same applies to debtEquity < 50 when equity is negative.
findings.fix: Guard every multiple with `> 0`, as done for pcf. Treat non-positive values as a penalty (e.g. `evEbitda <= 0 ? -1.5`, `pe <= 0 ? -2`) or exclude them from scoring and add the note 'EBITDA negativo' / 'capital contable negativo'. Mirror the same guards in the backend so the displayed ratios show 'N/A (negativo)'.
findings.verify_reasoning:
The main point holds for EV/EBITDA and P/B. It is overstated for P/E and D/E, and the proposed penalty for negative P/B is wrong on the finance side.

What I confirmed (src/App.jsx):
- In mlScoreStock (line 312), line 330 `if (evEbitda != null) val += evEbitda < 8 ? 1.5 ...`, line 331 `if (pb != null) val += pb < 1 ? 1 ...` and line 366 `if (pb != null) tech += pb < 1.5 ? 0.8 ...` have no > 0 guard. Line 332 does have one: `pcf != null && pcf > 0`.
- The data comes from `fetchStock`, which calls `/stock/{t}` (App.jsx 105-109) and ends up in `get_stock` (backend.py 1886). The score is used in the screener (App.jsx 1720) and the analysis view (App.jsx 4988).
- backend.py 318 `ev_ebitda = r2(safe(info.get("enterpriseToEbitda")))` and 287 `pb_val = r2(safe(info.get("priceToBook")))` pass Yahoo's values through unchanged. Yahoo does publish negative values: negative EV/EBITDA for companies losing money at the EBITDA level, and negative P/B for companies with negative book equity. The backend's own fallbacks do guard: line 343 requires `ebitda > 0 and ev_computed > 0`, and line 304 requires `bvps > 0`. So the unguarded primary path is inconsistent with the backend's own logic.
- Impact: a stock with negative EBITDA and P/B of about 3 gets val = 5 + 1.5 + 0.3 = 6.8, which rounds to 7. If the negative value is excluded, val is 5. That is 0.28 × 2 ≈ 0.56 on the overall score, enough to cross the rounding line at 4.5 or 6.5 and flip SELL↔HOLD or HOLD↔BUY. Medium severity is fair.
- The finding misses that the same flaw is in the display. MetricBadge at 3067-3068 (`good={12}` / `good={3}`, where v <= good means green) and the metrics array at 5001-5004 (`lo: v => v < 10`, `lo: v => v < 2`) show negative EV/EBITDA and negative P/B as green, i.e. "cheap".

What is overstated:
- P/E (line 327): backend.py 312-315 computes pe = price/eps only when `eps_val > 0`. Otherwise it falls back to Yahoo's trailingPE, which Yahoo leaves out when earnings are negative. A negative pe almost never reaches the frontend. A guard is still reasonable as a backstop, but this is not an active bug.
- D/E (lines 319, 348): Yahoo leaves out debtToEquity when equity is negative. The fallback at backend.py 294 requires `equity > 0`. So debtEquity < 0 is essentially unreachable, and the claim that D/E < 50 rewards negative equity is theoretical. The same applies to leverageRatio (backend.py 173-176).
- The fix's penalty for negative P/B is misapplied. Negative book equity often comes from buybacks at very profitable companies (MCD, SBUX, HD, AZO, BKNG, LOW), not from distress. P/B, like ROE and D/E, simply has no meaning when equity is negative. It should be excluded and flagged, not scored at -1 or -2.
- For negative EV/EBITDA, a large extra penalty double-counts: profitMargin < 0 already costs -2 in both fundamental and quality (lines 318, 347). Excluding it, or a small penalty, is enough. The weights in lines 327-332 also add up to much more than the valuation clamp allows, so deleting a term already shifts scores a lot.
findings.corrected_fix:
1) Scoring in src/App.jsx, mlScoreStock (lines 327-332, 366). Treat every multiple with a non-positive denominator as not meaningful:
```js
const pos = v => v != null && isFinite(v) && v > 0;
if (pos(pe)) val += pe < 12 ? 2.5 : ...;            // defense in depth; backend already only sends pe>0
if (pos(peg)) val += ...;  if (pos(pegy)) val += ...;
if (evEbitda != null) val += evEbitda > 0 ? (evEbitda < 8 ? 1.5 : evEbitda < 12 ? 0.7 : evEbitda < 18 ? 0 : evEbitda < 25 ? -0.7 : -1.5) : -0.5; // negative EBITDA: small penalty only, losses already penalized via profitMargin
if (pos(pb)) val += pb < 1 ? 1 : pb < 2.5 ? 0.3 : pb > 6 ? -0.8 : 0;   // pb<=0: skip, no reward and no penalty
...
if (pos(pb)) tech += pb < 1.5 ? 0.8 : pb > 8 ? -0.8 : 0;               // line 366
if (debtEquity != null && debtEquity >= 0) { ...lines 319/348... }      // cheap backstop
```
Add notes such as `if (evEbitda != null && evEbitda <= 0) notes.push("EBITDA negativo")` and `if (pb != null && pb <= 0) notes.push("capital contable negativo")`. For the negative P/B case, also skip the ROE terms (lines 317, 346), since ROE has no meaning when equity is negative.

2) Display. At lines 3064-3068 and 5001-5004, render values <= 0 for P/E, EV/EBITDA and P/B as "N/A (neg.)" in the muted color, not green. For example, in MetricBadge, if `v <= 0` and the badge is a multiple, set color to var(--muted). In the metrics array, change `lo` to `v => v > 0 && v < 10`.

3) Backend (backend.py 287, 318). Mirror the guards the fallbacks already use at lines 304 and 343. Set `ev_ebitda = None` when `<= 0` and `pb_val = None` when `<= 0`, and return flags such as `"ebitdaNegative": True` and `"negativeEquity": True` so the UI can explain why the value is missing instead of showing a misleading number.

findings.title: 'ML Screener' / 'ML Score' is a hand-tuned rule set that double-counts factors and issues BUY/SELL
findings.evidence: The header comment reads `// ─── ML SCORER (Rule-Based Quantitative Engine)`, yet the UI tab is 'ML Screener'. ROE, profitMargin, debtEquity and revenueGrowth each feed both `fund` (317-320) and `qual` (346-349). priceChange52w feeds both `mom` (338) and `tech` (358). pb feeds `val` and `tech`. 378: `overall_score >= 7 ? "BUY" : overall_score <= 4 ? "SELL" : "HOLD"`.
findings.why: No model is trained or validated, so calling it 'ML' misrepresents its evidentiary basis, a real problem when the product is given to employees. Double-counting means the stated 22/28/18/18/14 weights are not the real ones. The raw 52-week return effectively carries about 32% of the score, and profitability counts twice. Absolute P/E and EV/EBITDA cut-offs ignore sector (banks vs software) and country (BMV multiples run lower). 52-week momentum without skipping the latest month mixes in the 1-month reversal effect. BUY/SELL labels read as investment advice.
findings.fix: Rename it 'Score cuantitativo (reglas)' or 'Kaizen Score'. Use each input in only one pillar. Score factors as cross-sectional percentile ranks within sector and universe instead of fixed thresholds. Use 12-1 momentum. Replace BUY/HOLD/SELL with 'Atractivo alto/medio/bajo' plus a 'no es recomendación de inversión' disclaimer. Publish the methodology in a tooltip.
findings.verify_reasoning:
The core of the finding holds up when checked against the code. A few details are wrong, and the finding misses the worst double-count.

CONFIRMED:
- App.jsx:309 reads `// ─── ML SCORER (Rule-Based Quantitative Engine)`, and `mlScoreStock` (312-394) is a hard-coded if-ladder. Nothing is trained, fitted or validated.
- The 'ML' label is shown to users at 2177, 2230, 2261, 2274 ("ML Screener" tabs), 3521 (" Ejecutar ML Screener") and 5317 ("ML Score"). The helper text at 3533 more honestly says "Motor cuantitativo de scoring", which contradicts the button beside it.
- These inputs each feed two pillars:
  - roe (317 fund, 346 qual)
  - profitMargin (318, 347)
  - debtEquity (319, 348)
  - revenueGrowth (320, 349)
  - priceChange52w (338 mom, 358 tech)
  - pb (331 val, 366 tech)
- 378 is `overall_score >= 7 ? "BUY" : overall_score <= 4 ? "SELL" : "HOLD"`. It is shown as a colored badge at 3543/3564 (screener card, colored top border) and 5323 ("BUY · 8/10"). A grep for recomendación/disclaimer/asesor finds no investment disclaimer anywhere in App.jsx or ui.jsx.
- The thresholds are absolute and sector-blind, e.g. P/E<12 → +2.5 (327) and EV/EBITDA<8 (330). EV/EBITDA and D/E mean little for banks, and P/E and P/B are the wrong lens for FIBRAs/REITs (FFO/AFFO is the right one).
- The backend's priceChange52w is Yahoo's `52WeekChange`, or first-vs-last weekly close over 1y (backend.py:380-390). Either way it includes the latest month. The 12-1 convention (Jegadeesh-Titman; Carhart) skips that month because of the 1-month reversal (Jegadeesh 1990). So this point is valid.

WRONG OR OVERSTATED:
1. "The raw 52-week return effectively carries about 32% of the score" is inaccurate. 32% (0.18+0.14) is the combined weight of the two pillars where 52w is the main input, but beta and P/B also feed those pillars. Working from the ladders: 52w moves mom from 1.5 to 8 (6.5 pts × 0.18 = 1.17) and tech from 2.5 to 7.5 (5 pts × 0.14 = 0.70). That is about 1.9 points of the 1-10 composite, or roughly 20% of the range. The accurate claim is that 52w is the single most influential input, more than P/E alone (5 pts × 0.28 = 1.4).
2. The finding misses the worst case. backend.py:173-176 defines `_leverage_ratio(info)` as `1 + de / 100.0`. So leverageRatio is just debtEquity re-expressed, and one variable (D/E) is scored three times: 319 fund, 348 qual, 351 qual. That lets it move the composite by about 1.5 points. debtToAssets (322) adds a fourth, highly correlated leverage term.
3. The finding also misses that beta feeds both mom (341) and tech (363), with contradictory preferences. Mom rewards 0.7-1.4 and penalizes >2.5, while tech rewards <0.5 and penalizes >2. And the 'Técnico' pillar contains no technical indicator at all (no MA, RSI or trend-vs-MA). It is only 52w, beta and P/B, and the comment at 365 calls P/B "technical mean-reversion", which is a misnomer.
4. The proposed fix, "cross-sectional percentile ranks within sector and universe", does not fit this screener. The universe is whatever few tickers the user types into the textarea (3507; parsed at 1706). With 5 tickers across 4 sectors, within-sector percentiles are degenerate, and the same stock's score would change with its neighbors. Percentiles need a fixed reference universe on the backend.
5. Missing data is not handled well. Absent fields are skipped, so the pillar stays at 5. That pulls stocks with sparse Yahoo fundamentals (common for .MX tickers) toward "HOLD" and shows them with the same apparent confidence as fully covered stocks.

Severity: medium is appropriate. The labeling and double-counting are materially misleading but produce no numerically wrong prices or returns. It borders on high because BUY/SELL badges are handed to employees; that is a regulatory concern in Mexico, where CNBV regulates investment advice.
findings.corrected_fix:
1. Rename the feature.
   - Change the labels at App.jsx 2177, 2230, 2261, 2274, 3521 and 5317 to "Kaizen Score" or "Score cuantitativo (reglas)", and the button to "Ejecutar screener".
   - Change the comment at 309 and rename the function to `quantScoreStock`.

2. Make each raw input belong to exactly one pillar.
   - Valuation: pe, peg, pegy, evEbitda, pb, pcf.
   - Quality/profitability: roe, profitMargin.
   - Balance sheet: use debtEquity only, OR debtToAssets. Delete leverageRatio from 351, since backend.py:176 defines it as `1 + D/E/100`.
   - Growth: revenueGrowth.
   - Momentum: 12-1 return, which you can make sector-relative using the alpha that runScreener already fetches from /momentum at 1737 and that mlScoreStock currently ignores.
   - Risk: beta, or better, 1y volatility, in a single pillar with a single, consistent preference.
   - Delete the 'Técnico' pillar, or replace it with real technical signals (price vs 200-day MA, 50/200 cross) that do not reuse 52w or P/B.
   - Rebalance the weights so each factor's intended weight is its real weight.

3. Momentum:
   - In backend.py get_momentum, add `m12_1 = closes[-5]/closes[-53]-1` on the weekly series (skip about 4 weeks) and return it.
   - Use that instead of `52WeekChange` in the score.

4. Sector-aware scoring:
   - Do not rank within the user's typed list. Score each metric relative to a fixed reference: sector medians precomputed on the backend from a fixed universe (e.g. S&P 500 plus S&P/BMV IPC constituents), as z-scores or percentiles against that reference. Failing that, use per-sector threshold tables.
   - Exclude EV/EBITDA and D/E for Financials.
   - Score FIBRAs/REITs on P/FFO and dividend yield instead of P/E and P/B.

5. Coverage:
   - Return the count of available inputs per pillar.
   - Show "cobertura de datos: n/m". When coverage is below about 60%, grey the score out or label it "datos insuficientes" instead of letting it default to 5/HOLD.

6. Labels and disclaimer:
   - Replace BUY/HOLD/SELL at 378, 390, 3543-3564 and 5323 with neutral "Atractivo alto / medio / bajo", or show only the numeric score.
   - Add a visible disclaimer on the screener card and the Análisis panel: "Score cuantitativo basado en reglas; no es recomendación de inversión ni asesoría personalizada".
   - Apply the same wording to "RECOMENDACIONES PARA TU PORTAFOLIO" at 3436.

7. Methodology:
   - Add a methodology tooltip listing each pillar's inputs and real weights.
   - Stop rounding each pillar to an integer before the weighted sum (the clamp at 310 rounds). Round only the final score to one decimal.

findings.title: Cash ($MXN) is handled inconsistently: 0% return in backtest/Monte Carlo, excluded in optimizer and portfolio Sharpe
findings.evidence: 260: 'la caja ($MXN) pesa en el total pero rinde 0'. weightedReturns skips it (264) but its weight stays in the denominator (1499-1503, where stockData['$MXN'].price = 1). runOptimization filters it out (1323), and loadSharpeData skips it (1826), so its weights exclude cash (1848-1850).
findings.why: The same portfolio gets three different Sharpe ratios depending on the tab. At 0% return, cash contributes an excess return of −rf (about −7-9% a year in Mexico) per unit of weight, so the backtest Sharpe and alpha are penalized. Most Mexican investors keep 'efectivo' in CETES or money-market funds that earn close to rf.
findings.fix: Model $MXN as earning the weekly CETES rate (rf_t) in all tabs, with an option for 'efectivo sin rendimiento'. Include it consistently in weights everywhere, and in the optimizer as a fixed-weight or rf asset, which also lets you draw the Capital Market Line.

findings.title: Backtest stat cards ignore their colour argument; thresholds are dead code
findings.evidence: `const statCard = (label, value, unit) => (...color: "var(--accent)"...)` takes three parameters, but each call passes a fourth, e.g. `statCard("Alpha de Jensen", ..., "%", alpha >= 0 ? "var(--positive)" : "var(--negative)")`.
findings.why: Every metric renders in the same accent colour, so a negative alpha or a negative IR looks as 'good' as a positive one. Some of the intended thresholds are also questionable: `beta < 1 ? positive` treats low beta as intrinsically good, and `treynor > 0.1` is an arbitrary level.
findings.fix: Add a `color` parameter to statCard and use it. Colour only sign-meaningful metrics (alpha, IR, Sharpe versus the benchmark's Sharpe). Show beta and tracking error in neutral colours with a tooltip explaining the interpretation.

findings.title: Monte Carlo annualization exponent and horizon labelling are off; Sharpe shown with false precision
findings.evidence: 4478: `Math.pow(portMeanEnd, 52 / portStats.length) - 1`, where portStats.length = H+1 = 53, although the path spans exactly 52 weeks. The button says 'Ejecutar Monte Carlo (5 años)', but the horizon is 52 weeks (1651); 5 years is the length of history used. Sharpe is shown with `toFixed(4)` (3254, 3281, 3302, 4368). calcSharpe uses population variance (/n, line 167), while tracking error and beta use /(n−1) (255, 276).
findings.why: The 52/53 exponent understates the 1-year expected return by about 0.3pp at 15%. Users can read '5 años' as a 5-year projection. The standard error of a Sharpe ratio is about √((1+SR²/2)/years), roughly 0.45 for 5 years and 1.0 for 1 year, so four decimals imply precision that isn't there. Mixed variance estimators are a minor inconsistency.
findings.fix: Use `portMeanEnd - 1` (the horizon is 1 year), or `Math.pow(x, 52 / H)` generally. Relabel the button 'Simular 1 año (con 5 años de historial)'. Show Sharpe, Treynor and IR with 2 decimals plus a ± standard error or a 'baja significancia' hint. Standardize on the sample (n−1) variance.

findings.title: get_stock mixes trading currency and reporting currency in its fallback P/E, P/B and EV/EBITDA (it never reads financialCurrency)
findings.evidence: Price comes from info/fast_info/history in the trading currency (195-206). net_income, equity, total_debt and cash come from t.income_stmt/t.balance_sheet in the reporting currency (219-269). Then: `eps_val = round(net_income / shares_out, 4)` (309) followed by `pe = round(price / eps_val, 2)` (313). `bvps = equity / shares_out; pb_val = round(price / bvps, 2)` (303-305). `ev_computed = market_cap + (total_debt or 0) - (cash or 0)` (331), where market_cap is in the trading currency (286/298). A grep shows 'financialCurrency' is never used in get_stock; the only uses are in get_dcf and get_fibras.
findings.why: A price multiple needs the numerator and denominator in the same currency. The code itself expects .info to fail on cloud hosts ('puede ser lento o None en cloud', line 183), and when it does every fallback runs. For AAPL.MX (price in MXN, statements in USD), P/E and P/B come out roughly 18x too high (the USD/MXN rate). For an ADR like AMX (price in USD, statements in MXN) they come out about 18x too low. EV adds MXN market cap to USD debt. These numbers feed mlScoreStock (App.jsx 327-332: pe < 12 gives +2.5, pe ≥ 60 gives -2.5), so the BUY/SELL recommendation flips on a unit error. Mexican users hold US stocks mostly as .MX listings on the SIC, so this hits the core audience.
findings.fix: Read `fin_ccy = info.get('financialCurrency')` and `px_ccy = info.get('currency') or fast_info.currency`. If they differ, get the FX rate once (cached) and convert net_income, equity, total_debt, cash, EBITDA and FCF into the trading currency before computing any ratio against price or market cap. If fin_ccy cannot be determined (info empty), return None for P/E, P/B and EV/EBITDA instead of mixing currencies. Cache financialCurrency with a long TTL, since it almost never changes.
findings.verify_reasoning:
The core claim holds. get_stock (backend.py 179-438) never reads financialCurrency. The only place it gets the rate needed to convert statement figures into the trading currency is get_dcf (863-878, 929-939) and get_fibras (1586-1598). In get_stock, price is in the trading currency (195-206). net_income, equity, total_debt and cash are in the reporting currency, whether they come from info netIncomeToCommon/totalDebt/totalCash (220-222, 322) or from income_stmt/balance_sheet (238-259, 323-328). Three fallbacks mix them: `eps_val = round(net_income / shares_out, 4)` then `pe = round(price / eps_val, 2)` (308-313); `bvps = equity / shares_out; pb_val = round(price / bvps, 2)` (302-305); `ev_computed = market_cap + (total_debt or 0) - (cash or 0)` (330-331), where market_cap comes from info marketCap or fast_info.market_cap (286, 298), both in the trading currency. The scoring impact is also real. mlScoreStock (App.jsx 312, with the pe/evEbitda/pb bands at about lines 326-330) turns these into valuation points, and the screener (App.jsx 1720) and the analysis view (4988) both use it.

Details that are wrong or overstated:

1. **Scope is misdescribed.** Having .info does not make P/E safe. get_dcf's own comment (922-924) says Yahoo returns trailingEps and bookValue already in the trading currency. So when trailingEps is present, `price / eps_val` (312-313) is fine; that is the normal path. The mixing does NOT need .info to fail, though. With .info present but trailingEps missing and netIncomeToCommon present, EPS comes out in the reporting currency (308). With .info present but enterpriseToEbitda missing, EV adds info marketCap (trading) to info totalDebt/totalCash (reporting). In both cases financialCurrency was available in `info` and simply ignored.

2. **When .info is empty, the bug only fires if fast_info.shares returns a value** (277). Without it, shares_out is None, the P/E and P/B fallbacks are skipped, and fast_info.market_cap (which is derived from shares) is also None, so EV is skipped too. For many .MX SIC listings Yahoo has no share count, so this path is conditional, not guaranteed. I would rate it high, not critical.

3. **The AMX '18x too low' figure ignores the ADR ratio.** One AMX ADS is a multiple of ordinary shares, and Yahoo's share count may be in ordinary shares. The FX error and the ratio error can partly cancel, so the size of the error is not simply 1/FX. The AAPL.MX example (MXN price, USD statements, roughly FX-times too high) is the valid one.

4. **Missed, same root cause.** Line 437 `"currency": info.get("currency", "USD")` labels an .MX price as USD whenever .info is empty. The raw fields returned at 426-431 (netIncomeToCommon, totalDebt, freeCashflow, totalRevenue) are in the reporting currency, marketCap (420) is in the trading currency, and all of them sit under that one currency label.

5. **The proposed fix has a gap.** It says to use `fast_info.currency` when .info is empty. That gives the trading currency, but financialCurrency is only available from .info, so the 'if they differ' comparison cannot run. You cannot infer it from the .MX suffix either: Mexican issuers report in MXN, while SIC listings of US companies report in USD.

findings.title: get_dcf assumes 'USD' when financialCurrency is missing, and trusts that trailingEps/bookValue are in the trading currency without checking
findings.evidence: `financial_currency = info.get("financialCurrency", "USD") or "USD"` (864). For a Mexican company with price_currency MXN and a missing financialCurrency field, pair becomes 'USDMXN=X' and fx_rate is about 18. Then `fcf = fcf_fin * fx_rate` (931), `ev = ev_fin * fx_rate` (935) and `cash_l/debt_l *= fx_rate` (938-939), which inflates the P/FCF and EV/EBITDA targets about 18x. Separately, lines 922-926 assert that EPS and bookValue are already in the trading currency ('NO aplicar conversión de moneda') and use them directly, together with `shares = info['sharesOutstanding']` (912).
findings.why: The per-share targets are only valid if EPS, BVPS, FCF per share and price share one currency and one share unit. A missing field should mean 'same currency as the price', not 'USD'. For ADRs, Yahoo's bookValue is often in the reporting currency (a known yfinance pitfall that produces nonsense P/B for foreign ADRs). sharesOutstanding may be ordinary shares while the price is per ADS, which breaks FCF per share. If trailingEps for AAPL.MX is in USD, the P/E target is about 6.4 x 28 = 179 'MXN' against a price of about 4,000, a margin of about -2,000%.
findings.fix: Use `financial_currency = info.get('financialCurrency') or price_currency`. Before using trailingEps or bookValue, check their units: compute `eps_fin = netIncomeToCommon / shares` and look at trailingEps/eps_fin. A ratio near 1 means it is in the reporting currency and should be multiplied by fx_rate; a ratio near fx_rate means it is already in the trading currency. Do the same for bookValue against totalStockholderEquity/shares. Get per-share figures with implied shares = marketCap/price (both in the trading currency), which also absorbs ADR ratios. Build EV yourself as marketCap + (debt - cash) x fx rather than trusting the currency of Yahoo's enterpriseValue.

- That 18 then multiplies freeCashflow (line 931, and so fcf_ps at 932), enterpriseValue (935), cash (938) and debt (939). EBITDA per share comes from ev/ev_eb (972-973) and is 18x too. net_cash_ps (941) is 18x as well. So the P/FCF target (964) and the EV/EBITDA target (974) are both about 18x too high.

- The default is also inconsistent within the codebase: the FIBRA code at line 1587 defaults the same field to "MXN".
- The docstring (lines 811-812) says per-share EPS, BVPS and FCF are multiplied by fx_rate. The comment at lines 922-924 says the opposite ("NO aplicar conversión de moneda"). So the author's own documentation contradicts the code, and nothing in the code checks units.

Here that value is multiplied by up to 8x (Technology P/B) and treated as a target in the trading currency. The core point stands, and "high" severity is fair.

What is overstated:
1. The ADS share-count claim is speculative. For large US ADRs, Yahoo's sharesOutstanding is usually ADS-equivalent, so marketCap ≈ price x shares holds. BMV SIC cross-listings are 1:1.
2. The AAPL.MX EPS example is written as a hypothetical ("If trailingEps ... is in USD"). It is not demonstrated. Yahoo usually does normalize trailingEps for ADRs; bookValue is the field that is commonly wrong.
3. How often financialCurrency is actually missing for .MX names can't be checked read-only. When Yahoo leaves it out, other fundamentals are often missing too.

What is wrong in the fix:
- Defaulting to price_currency is not safe either. For a SIC listing such as AAPL.MX, a missing field would then treat USD FCF, cash and debt as MXN, and the P/FCF and EV/EBITDA targets would be about 18x too low. A missing currency should be treated as unknown, not silently replaced with either value.

findings.title: Momentum 'alpha' compares .MX stocks in MXN with US sector ETFs in USD, so peso moves show up as alpha
findings.evidence: `etf = SECTOR_ETF.get(sector, "SPY")` maps every stock to XLK/XLF/XLRE and so on. `hist_stock = yft(ticker).history(...)` is in the ticker's own currency (MXN for .MX), while `hist_etf` is in USD. Then `alpha_12m = stock_12m - etf_12m` (1741) and `score = sum(a > 0)` (1744).
findings.why: Excess return is only meaningful when both returns are in the same currency. In MXN terms the ETF's return is about r_USD + Δ(USD/MXN), so the reported 'alpha' is off by roughly the peso's move. In 2024 USD/MXN rose about 22% (from about 17 to about 20.8), so every .MX stock and every SIC listing such as AAPL.MX showed roughly 20 points of fake 12-month outperformance. For a Mexican stock, a US sector ETF is also the wrong peer group. The error flows into the screener's momentum column (App.jsx 3679) and the score.
findings.fix: Measure both series in one currency. For .MX tickers, either convert the ETF series to MXN with the MXN=X history already cached in get_chart (reuse its alignment code), or benchmark Mexican issuers against ^MXX or NAFTRAC.MX. For US companies listed on the SIC (AAPL.MX), benchmark the underlying US ticker against the US ETF in USD. Return a `benchmarkCurrency` field.

findings.title: Fair value uses static US sector multiples for every stock, including Mexican ones, ignoring country risk and each firm's growth and ROE
findings.evidence: Hard-coded tables `SECTOR_PE = {"Technology":28, ..., "Consumer Defensive":22, ...}` labeled 'Damodaran Jan 2025', with no market or date awareness. `pe_fair = SECTOR_PE.get(sector, 18)`, and then the same fixed multiple applies to WALMEX.MX, AMXB.MX and AAPL. `fair_price = ... sum(targets)/len(methods)` is a plain average.
findings.why: The justified multiple is P/E = payout x (1+g)/(r - g). Mexican equities carry a higher cost of equity: M10 is about 8.6% against about 4% for the US 10-year, plus a country risk premium. That is why the IPC has historically traded around 11-14x earnings against 20x+ for the S&P 500. Applying US medians to Mexican firms makes nearly every BMV stock look INFRAVALORADO. The fixed tables are also 20 months old, and Yahoo's 11 sectors don't match Damodaran's roughly 94 industries, so the attribution can't be verified. An unweighted mean also lets a single outlier (for example P/B = 8x for tech) dominate.
findings.fix: Keep separate multiple tables per market: US, and Mexico/emerging markets (from Damodaran's Emerging Markets dataset, or better, live medians computed daily from the app's own BMV and US universes). At minimum, adjust with the firm's fundamentals: justified P/B = (ROE - g)/(Re - g) and justified P/E = payout(1+g)/(Re - g), using the market's own Re. Aggregate targets with the median, show the spread between methods (min to max) as a confidence band, and stamp the source and date in the response.
findings.verify_reasoning:
The main point is correct, but several details, the economic argument and the proposed fix need fixing.

What I confirmed in backend.py:
- **Static tables.** Lines 821-841 define SECTOR_PE, SECTOR_PB, SECTOR_PFCF and SECTOR_EV_EBITDA as module-level constants in get_dcf, labeled "Damodaran Jan 2025". Nothing in them depends on market, country, date or the firm's own ROE, growth or payout.
- **Same multiple for everyone.** Lines 943-946 look up `pe_fair = SECTOR_PE.get(sector, 18)` and similar by Yahoo sector only. WALMEX.MX, FUNO11.MX and AAPL get identical multiples.
- **Plain mean.** Line 986 is `fair_price = sum(targets)/len(methods)`.
- **Displayed with no provenance.** The frontend shows the result on every portfolio position (App.jsx 1261 fetches /dcf per holding; the card at 3082-3150) and in the screener (3643-3670). It shows "vs sector {m.fair}x" and INFRAVALORADO/SOBREVALORADO with no source, date or market attached.
- **Staleness.** Jan 2025 to Sep 2026 is 20 months. Damodaran publishes about 94 US industries, not Yahoo's 11 sectors, so the attribution can't be verified.
- **The app contradicts itself on real estate.** SECTOR_PB["Real Estate"]=1.5 means a FIBRA at 0.6x book gets a P/B target of about 2.5x its price. The app's own FIBRA screener (lines 1477-1480) treats P/NAV 0.85-1.15 as fair value. FIBRA net income under IFRS also includes fair-value revaluation gains, so a 30x P/E on it is meaningless.

This is wrong or overstated in the finding:
1. **"Nearly every BMV stock looks INFRAVALORADO" is too strong.** The bias does lean toward undervalued for Mexican issuers. But the overall label is a majority vote of per-method signals first (lines 990-997), and the margin decides only when there is no majority. High-multiple names like WALMEX (historically about 20x+ P/E, 5-6x P/B) come out near fair. Banks come out mixed: P/E says cheap against 12x, P/B says expensive against 1.4x. FIBRAs, miners and cement names are where the bias is large.
2. **The cost-of-equity argument mixes inflation with risk.** "M10 8.6% vs UST 4%" is mostly an expected-inflation gap. Higher expected inflation also raises nominal growth in P/E = payout(1+g)/(Re-g), so it largely cancels out. The real sources of Mexico's discount are the country risk premium and lower ROE and growth. Also, "M10 plus a CRP" double counts: M10 already contains the sovereign default spread. The Damodaran approach is either local Rf = M10 minus the default spread, plus beta x (mature ERP + CRP), or US Rf + beta x (mature ERP + CRP), converted to MXN with the inflation differential.
3. **Splitting by ".MX" suffix would break SIC listings.** Tickers like AAPL.MX and AMZN.MX are US companies quoted in MXN on the SIC. The code already overrides AMZN.MX and META.MX (lines 892-906) and handles FX for them. The market choice must use the issuer's domicile (info["country"]), not the ticker suffix.
4. **The outlier example points at the wrong thing.** A tech P/B of 8x is not the outlier. The outlier comes from the per-share input: buyback-heavy or asset-light firms (for example AAPL, with tiny book value) get a P/B target far below their P/E and P/FCF targets. A median helps, but the real fix is to drop methods that don't apply to a sector.

Severity "high" is fair. These labels appear on users' own holdings and would be acted on.

findings.title: Multiples valuation is applied to FIBRAs and banks where the methods don't apply
findings.evidence: 'Real Estate' gets P/E 30, P/B 1.5, P/FCF 22 and EV/EBITDA 18. 'Financial Services' gets P/FCF 14 and EV/EBITDA 14. Only ETFs and funds are excluded (847-848); FIBRAs have quoteType EQUITY. The frontend calls /dcf for every holding (App.jsx 1261) and in the screener (App.jsx 1736), even though a dedicated get_fibras model with P/NAV exists (backend.py 1458-1466, 1624).
findings.why: FIBRAs report under IFRS: their net income includes fair-value revaluations of investment property and FX gains or losses on USD debt, so P/E x 30 is meaningless. FIBRAs typically trade at 0.5-0.8x book, so a 1.5x P/B target labels essentially every FIBRA (FUNO11, FIBRAPL14 and others) 'barato', with a 'discount' of 50% or more. For banks, debt is raw material and operating cash flow is swamped by deposit and loan flows, so FCF and EV/EBITDA are not valid measures (Damodaran, Investment Valuation, ch. 21). The standard tools for banks are P/E and P/B justified by ROE.
findings.fix: Route by business type. For FIBRAs/REITs (a ticker in FIBRAS_LIST, or sector Real Estate with quoteType EQUITY on .MX), return the get_fibras metrics instead: P/NAV, AFFO/FFO yield and distribution yield vs M10. For Financial Services, use only P/E and justified P/B = (ROE - g)/(Re - g), and drop P/FCF and EV/EBITDA. Report the methods used and why the others were excluded.

- The app also contradicts itself. get_fibras treats P/NAV of 0.85-1.15 as fair value (lines 1623-1625), which anchors on 1.0x book. /dcf targets 1.5x book, so any FIBRA with P/B below 1.275 gets a P/B "barato" badge. For P/B between 0.85 and 1.275, the FIBRA Screener says PRECIO JUSTO (or CARA above 1.15) while the portfolio card says barato, for the same ticker.
- The P/E criticism is valid. Mexican FIBRAs use the IAS 40 fair-value model, so trailing EPS includes revaluation gains and FX gains or losses on USD debt. Multiplying that by 30 is noise.

What is wrong or overstated:
1. EV/EBITDA is a standard REIT metric (Nareit's EBITDAre), so it is not "inapplicable." P/FCF is roughly a P/AFFO proxy, and the app's own get_fibras uses FCF / market cap as its FFO yield. For those two methods the real problem is the level: 22x FCF and 18x EBITDA are US medians. FIBRAs priced off an M10 of about 9-10% trade closer to 8-12x AFFO. Yahoo's EBITDA for IFRS filers may also include revaluation gains.
2. P/B is not the wrong tool for FIBRAs. Under IAS 40, book value is roughly NAV, so P/B is P/NAV, which is the correct REIT metric. The error is the 1.5x anchor. That level suits US REITs, whose GAAP book is depreciated historical cost. For IFRS FIBRAs the anchor should be about 1.0x.
3. "A discount of 50% or more" only applies to the P/B method on its own. The headline `margin` averages all methods (lines 985-987), so the discount users see depends on the other methods too.
4. FIBRAPL14 is a weak example. It reports in USD, and the code does not convert bookValue or EPS (lines 922-926), so its P/B result depends on which currency Yahoo uses for bookValue. It could come out "caro" instead. FUNO11, which reports in MXN, is the clean example.
5. For banks, EV/EBITDA rarely fires, because line 971 requires `enterpriseToEbitda` and Yahoo seldom provides it for banks. The real risk is P/FCF (line 963): any positive FCF, driven by deposit and loan flows, produces a nonsense target. Medium severity for banks, versus high for FIBRAs.
6. The Financial Services fix is wrong as written. Yahoo puts V, MA, AXP, PYPL, SPGI, MCO, CME and BLK in that sector (industries such as Credit Services, Capital Markets, Financial Data & Stock Exchanges and Asset Management). Leaving them only P/E 12 and a bank-style P/B would label them SOBREVALORADO. Routing has to use `info.get("industry")`, not the sector. The same goes for Real Estate: developers and real estate services firms (for example CBRE) are not REITs.
findings.corrected_fix:
All changes go in backend.py get_dcf, after the sector is resolved (around line 910).

1. Classify by industry, not sector:
   - `industry = info.get("industry") or ""`
   - `is_reit = ticker_upper in FIBRAS_LIST or industry.startswith("REIT") or "FIBRA" in (info.get("longName") or "").upper()`
   - `is_bank = industry.startswith("Banks") or industry.startswith("Insurance")`
   - Every other Financial Services industry (Credit Services, Capital Markets, Exchanges, Asset Management) and non-REIT Real Estate keeps the general model, but with industry-appropriate multiples, not bank ones.

2. REIT branch:

   - P/NAV: for IFRS fair-value filers (.MX FIBRAs), use book value per share as NAV with a 1.0x anchor and the same 0.85/1.15 thresholds as get_fibras. Move that logic into a shared helper so /dcf and /fibras can never disagree. For US GAAP REITs, omit P/B or use a separate anchor, because their book is historical cost.
   - AFFO proxy: FCF per share (keep the existing FX guard). Set the target from a required yield, not a US multiple: `target = FCF_ps / (local_rf + spread)`, with local_rf = M10 for .MX tickers and UST10 for US tickers.
   - Report distribution yield minus the local 10-year yield as a spread.

3. Bank and insurer branch:
   - Keep P/E.
   - Add justified P/B = (ROE − g) / (Re − g), where:
     - ROE = `info["returnOnEquity"]`
     - Re = local rf + beta × ERP (plus country risk premium for .MX)
     - g is capped at long-run nominal GDP
     - Require ROE to be present and Re > g.
   - Drop P/FCF and EV/EBITDA.

4. Response and frontend:
   - Return `model: "reit" | "bank" | "general"` and `methodsExcluded: [{name, reason}]`.
   - In App.jsx 3082-3160 (portfolio card) and 3643-3665 (screener), show the model used, the excluded methods with their reasons, and for FIBRAs a link to the FIBRA Screener instead of the generic "VALUACIÓN POR MÚLTIPLOS" block.
   - Don't show an INFRAVALORADO or SOBREVALORADO verdict when fewer than 2 valid methods remain.

Severity: high for FIBRAs (core Mexican users, and signals that contradict the app's own FIBRA Screener); medium for banks.

findings.title: Every Sharpe ratio uses the 10-year Bono M yield as the risk-free rate instead of the short-term CETES rate
findings.evidence: get_rf returns `IRLTLT01MXM156N` (10-year government bond yield, OECD monthly). The frontend feeds it into calcSharpe as `rf_weekly = rf_annual / 52` (App.jsx 162-170) and into the optimizer, Monte Carlo and screener Sharpe (App.jsx 1341, 1533, 1707, 1823). The failure path is never cached (line 1841 returns without _cache_put), so every /rf call during a FRED outage waits for the 8-second timeout again.
findings.why: The Sharpe ratio's risk-free rate must be riskless over the measurement interval, a weekly return here. That is a short-term bill (CETES 28 days), not a 10-year bond whose price moves week to week and which carries a term premium. When the yield curve slopes up, Sharpe is understated; when it inverts (2023: CETES 28d about 11.3% vs M10 about 9.5%), Sharpe is overstated. The rf also shifts the tangency (max-Sharpe) portfolio the optimizer recommends. The 10-year yield is correct for CAPM and DCF discount rates, just not here.
findings.fix: Return two rates: `rf_short` (CETES 28 days, from Banxico SIE with a free token, e.g. series SF43936, or FRED INTGSTMXM193N / IR3TIB01MXM156N without a token) for Sharpe, Sortino and Monte Carlo, and `rf_long` (M10, as now) for CAPM and DCF. Include both labels and asOf dates. Cache the fallback for about 10 minutes and serve the last good value before the fixed constant.
findings.verify_reasoning:
The main point holds. /Users/luisalfredolizarragasanchez/Desktop/CLAUDE/05 NEWKAIZEN/backend.py lines 1814-1841: get_rf fetches FRED IRLTLT01MXM156N, the OECD monthly 10-year yield, labelled "Bono M 10Y". It is served at /rf (line 1890) and fetched once when the app mounts (App.jsx 1233-1234). It then drives every excess-return calculation:
- calcSharpe (App.jsx 162-170, `rf_weekly = rf_annual / 52`)
- sharpeOf (1306-1313)
- calcPortfolioSharpe and optimizeSharpe, the 100k-portfolio max-Sharpe search (172-181, 206-246, called at 1341-1403 and 1852)
- the screener Sharpe (1707, 1728)
- the per-holding Sharpe (1823, 1831)
- the backtest block (1533-1539)

The returns are weekly MXN returns (get_chart ccy=MXN, backend 479-513), so there is no currency mismatch. What remains is a maturity mismatch. The Sharpe numerator should be the return over the rate on a riskless asset for the same holding period, which is a bill (CETES 28d), not a 10-year bond that carries a term premium and duration risk. With today's positively sloped Mexican curve (M10 about 8.6% vs CETES about 7%), every Sharpe is understated by roughly (1.6%)/σ, and the max-Sharpe portfolio shifts, since the tangency point depends on rf. Medium severity is fair: the label is shown in the UI (2206-2209, 3205, 3313), so it is disclosed, but the default choice is still wrong.

The caching claim is also confirmed. The fallback return at line 1841 never calls _cache_put, and neither does the out-of-range `break`. So during a FRED outage every /rf call blocks a ThreadingHTTPServer thread for up to the 8s timeout. In practice that happens once per page load, and it holds back loadSharpeData, which waits for rfRate !== null (App.jsx 1866).

Where the finding is wrong:
1. There is no Sortino anywhere in App.jsx. runMonteCarlo (1574+) does not use rf at all. App.jsx 1533 is the backtest, not Monte Carlo; the only "Monte Carlo" that uses rf is the optimizer.
2. Sending rf_long to "CAPM and DCF" does not match this code. get_dcf does not use /rf. The only CAPM-type consumers are calcTreynor and calcJensensAlpha (281-292, called at 1536-1537). Those are ex-post performance measures on weekly returns, so by the same reasoning they must use the short rate. The 10-year yield only belongs in an ex-ante cost of equity or DCF discount rate, which does not consume /rf today.
3. The suggested FRED series are imperfect. IR3TIB01MXM156N is the OECD 3-month interbank rate, a TIIE-like proxy that typically sits a few tens of basis points above CETES 28, not CETES itself. INTGSTMXM193N is an IMF IFS series that may be stale or discontinued on FRED. Banxico SIE SF43936 (CETES 28-day auction yield, free Bmx-Token) is the right primary source.
4. A further refinement: the code subtracts today's spot rate from windows of 1 to 10 years. Banxico's rate went from about 4% in 2021 to 11.25% in 2023 to about 7% now. For ex-post Sharpe on a 5y lookback, the average short rate over the window (or the weekly CETES series matched to each week) is the correct benchmark, not today's rate.

Minor: the rfLabel initial state is "MX 5Y" (App.jsx 1048), which contradicts the backend label. The 0.0860 fallback is hard-coded in five places (155, 1341, 1533, 1707, 1823) plus backend 1841.
findings.corrected_fix:
Backend (backend.py 1814-1841):
1. Split get_rf into `_rf_short()` and `_rf_long()`.
   - `_rf_short()`: primary source is Banxico SIE `https://www.banxico.org.mx/SieAPIRest/service/v1/series/SF43936/datos/oportuno` with header `Bmx-Token` from `os.environ["BANXICO_TOKEN"]`. Token-free fallback: FRED `IR3TIB01MXM156N`, labelled honestly as "TIIE/interbancaria 3M (proxy)".

2. Keep the long rate only for a future ex-ante cost-of-equity/DCF input (nothing uses /rf that way today).

4. Convert with the compounding-consistent weekly rate `(1+rf)^(1/52)-1` rather than `rf/52`.
